text.en: Raju checked the weather before leaving. "What is air made of?" he asked.

The atmosphere is the layer of gases around the Earth. Dry air is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen, with small amounts of other gases. Water vapour in the atmosphere varies. Its layers are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. Weather happens in the troposphere.
Weather elements are temperature, pressure, winds, humidity and rainfall. Climate describes the long-term patterns of weather, including typical conditions, variation and extremes. Air tends to accelerate from higher toward lower pressure. Earth’s rotation and surface friction affect wind direction. Rainfall can develop when air is lifted by terrain, local heating or larger weather systems.
The ozone in the stratosphere shields us from ultraviolet rays. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations increase the greenhouse effect and warm the climate.

Air tends to accelerate from higher toward lower pressure. Earth’s rotation and surface friction affect wind direction. Rainfall can develop when air is lifted by terrain, local heating or larger weather systems.
The ozone in the stratosphere shields us from ultraviolet rays.
The atmosphere is held around Earth by gravity. Air is densest near the surface, where the weight of air above compresses it.

board.text: Air density generally decreases with height

text.en: Nitrogen and oxygen make up most dry air. Argon and carbon dioxide are among the other gases. The amount of water vapour can change from place to place and hour to hour.

board.text: Dry air proportions exclude water vapour

text.en: Much solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground. The surface then transfers energy to the air and emits infrared radiation.
Nearly all ordinary weather develops in the troposphere. The height of its upper boundary varies by latitude and season, so its top is not at one fixed altitude.
The stratosphere contains the main ozone layer. Ozone absorbs much ultraviolet radiation. This absorption also helps explain why temperature rises with height through much of the stratosphere.
Above the stratosphere lie the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. In the uppermost region, the atmosphere becomes extremely thin and gradually merges with space.

board.text: Five layers give a vertical reference

text.en: A hot afternoon and a cool night are observations of weather. To describe climate, compare observations over many years and look for patterns in conditions such as seasonal rainfall.

board.text: Weather: current or recent · climate: long-term patterns

text.en: Coastal and inland places at similar latitudes can have different temperatures. Water often changes temperature more slowly than nearby land, which can moderate coastal conditions.

board.text: Coasts often have smaller temperature ranges

text.en: Thermometers measure temperature and barometers measure air pressure. A rain gauge records the depth of liquid precipitation collected at a place over a time interval.

board.text: Choose the instrument for the quantity

text.en: On a weather map, an isobar connects places with the same air pressure. Lines close together show a stronger pressure change over a short distance.
A pressure difference can start air moving. As air moves, Earth’s rotation changes its path relative to the ground. Near the surface, friction also affects speed and direction.

board.text: Wind depends on pressure, rotation and friction

text.en: Trade winds and westerlies are examples of broad wind belts. Their directions describe general patterns. Actual wind at a place can vary with weather and terrain.
Monsoon winds change direction with the seasons. Contrasts in heating between land and sea contribute to the changes, along with larger atmospheric circulation.
A sea breeze can blow inland in the afternoon when land heats faster than water. At night, a land breeze can develop in the other direction under favourable conditions.

board.text: Daytime sea breeze can blow toward land

text.en: Clouds are made of small water droplets, ice crystals or both. Thin cirrus clouds usually form high up. Stratus clouds form layers, and cumulus often looks like rounded heaps.

board.text: Cloud forms include cirrus, stratus and cumulus

text.en: Relative humidity compares the water vapour actually present with the amount needed for saturation at that temperature. Changing temperature can change relative humidity even if the amount of vapour stays the same.
When air cools to its dew point, it reaches saturation under the same pressure and vapour conditions. Further cooling may lead to condensation. Near the ground, tiny suspended droplets can form fog.

board.text: Cooling can lead to saturation and condensation

text.en: Convectional rain can develop when strongly warmed surface air rises and cools. A rising cloud can grow vertically if conditions support continued upward motion.

Relief rain can develop when a hill or mountain forces moist air upward. Some places on the downwind side receive less rain because the descending air can warm and become less humid relative to saturation.
Cyclonic or frontal rainfall is associated with lifting in larger weather systems. In a front, warmer air can be lifted where it meets cooler air. Cooling helps clouds and rain develop.

board.text: Larger weather systems can lift air

text.en: Separate the ozone layer from the greenhouse effect. Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Greenhouse gases affect how infrared radiation escapes to space, and rising greenhouse gas concentrations warm the climate.

board.text: Ultraviolet absorption and infrared absorption are different

text.en: For a final comparison, choose one pathway by which air rises. Trace rising, cooling and condensation. Then name the evidence you would look for to classify the rainfall.

board.text: Cause of lift → cooling → cloud or rain

problem.en: Moist air moves up the first side of a mountain. Explain why the first slope can receive more rain than the far side.

text.en: Follow the wind up the first slope, where the air expands and cools.

why.en: Cooling can cause water vapour to condense and contribute to rain.

text.en: Follow the air as it descends behind the mountain.

why.en: Descending air warms. Rain can be less likely there, producing a rain shadow.

prompt.en: A friend says Weather and climate mean the same. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Weather is for a short time.

points.en: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen.
